2.1 Continuous-time transitions and process covariance
The transition matrix is \(\Phi_k = \exp(A\,\Delta t_k)\) with entries derived in the matrix exponential section below. For each branch \(b \in \{p, s\}\), the process covariance of \((x_b, I_b)\) over an interval of length \(\Delta t_k\) has the block form \(\begin{bmatrix} q^{b}_{xx} & q^{b}_{xI} \\ q^{b}_{xI} & q^{b}_{II} \end{bmatrix}\). Writing \(x = \kappa_b\,\Delta t_k\) and using \(\sigma_b^2 = 2\kappa_b V_b\), the entries are
\[
\begin{aligned}
q^{b}_{xx} &= V_b\left(1 - e^{-2x}\right), \\
q^{b}_{xI} &= \frac{V_b}{\kappa_b}\left(1 - e^{-x}\right)^2, \\
q^{b}_{II} &= \frac{V_b}{\kappa_b^2}\left(2x - 3 + 4e^{-x} - e^{-2x}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
The covariance is block-diagonal across branches because the drives are independent. When \(x < 10^{-3}\), the exponential differences suffer catastrophic cancellation, and truncated Taylor expansions in \(\Delta t_k\) are used instead:
\[
\begin{aligned}
q^{b}_{xx} &\approx 2\kappa_b V_b\left[\Delta t_k - \kappa_b \Delta t_k^2 + \tfrac{2}{3}\kappa_b^2 \Delta t_k^3\right], \\
q^{b}_{xI} &\approx 2\kappa_b V_b\left[\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta t_k^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}\kappa_b \Delta t_k^3 + \tfrac{7}{24}\kappa_b^2 \Delta t_k^4\right], \\
q^{b}_{II} &\approx 2\kappa_b V_b\left[\tfrac{1}{3}\Delta t_k^3 - \tfrac{1}{4}\kappa_b \Delta t_k^4 + \tfrac{7}{60}\kappa_b^2 \Delta t_k^5\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
For the vagal branch, \(V_p = \lambda_P\) (constant within a recording).

title: Supplementary material
section: 2.2 Dual-filter recursion, Joseph update and phase reset
text:
2.2 Dual-filter recursion, Joseph update and phase reset
Two filters are run in parallel and share one covariance recursion and Kalman gain. The stochastic filter \(\tilde{X}^{(0)}\) treats the observation as \(y_k = 1\) (that is, \(\nu_0 = 0\)), and the deterministic filter \(\tilde{X}^{(\nu)}\) treats it as \(y_k = \Delta t_k\) (the unit-\(\nu_0\) response). Both start from zero, with initial covariance \(P_0 = \mathrm{diag}(\lambda_P,\ 1,\ 0,\ 0)\), which is the stationary covariance of the drives and zero for the phase integrals. At each beat:

Prediction. \(\tilde{X}_{k|k-1} = \Phi_k \tilde{X}_{k-1|k-1}\) for both filters, and \(P_{k|k-1} = \Phi_k P_{k-1|k-1}\Phi_k^\top + Q_k\).
Innovation variance and gain. With the threshold-noise variance \(R_k = \lambda_R\,\mu_k\,\Delta t_k\), where \(\mu_k\) is the artifact multiplier defined below, \(S_k = H P_{k|k-1} H^\top + R_k\) (floored at \(10^{-12}\)) and \(K_k = P_{k|k-1}H^\top / S_k\).
Innovations. \(v_k^{(0)} = 1 - H\tilde{X}^{(0)}_{k|k-1}\) and \(v_k^{(\nu)} = \Delta t_k - H\tilde{X}^{(\nu)}_{k|k-1}\).
Update. \(\tilde{X}_{k|k} = \tilde{X}_{k|k-1} + K_k v_k\) for each filter, and the Joseph form \[
P_{k|k} = (I - K_k H)\,P_{k|k-1}\,(I - K_k H)^\top + K_k R_k K_k^\top,
\] followed by symmetrization, \(P_{k|k} \leftarrow (P_{k|k} + P_{k|k}^\top)/2\).
Storage and phase reset. The posterior states and covariance are stored and the integral components (\(I_p\), \(I_s\)) of both state vectors and the corresponding rows and columns of \(P_{k|k}\) are set to zero, whereas \(x_p\), \(x_s\) and their covariances are propagated unchanged to the next interval.

The measurement-noise term \(R_k\) contains only the threshold-level jitter. The uncertainty in the integrated drives is carried by \(H P_{k|k-1} H^\top\) and enters \(S_k\) but not the Joseph noise term. \(R_k\) represents the timing jitter of the depolarization threshold and the timing error of the acquisition system. The Joseph form preserves symmetry and positive semidefiniteness of \(P_{k|k}\) under finite-precision arithmetic.
Artifact multiplier. Let \(J_k = \max\left(|\Delta t_k - \Delta t_{k-1}|/\Delta t_{k-1},\ |\Delta t_{k+1} - \Delta t_k|/\Delta t_k\right)\) be the largest relative change between adjacent intervals at beat \(k\) (one-sided at the ends of the series). The multiplier is \(\mu_k = \min\{1 + (J_k/\theta_J)^{p_J},\ 10^{10}\}\) with \(\theta_J = 0.25\) and \(p_J = 10\), and the inflated jitter variance is capped at \(10^{12}\). As \(\mu_k\) increases, \(K_k \to 0\) and the observation has a negligible effect on the states. The multiplier references both adjacent intervals and is therefore not strictly causal; it affects only the observation-noise weighting and not the dynamics of the latent drives. Beats with \(\mu_k \ge 100\) are excluded from \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\) and the likelihood.

title: Supplementary material
section: 2.3 GLS profiling and reconstruction of the states
text:
2.3 GLS profiling and reconstruction of the states
Because \(\nu_0\) enters the observation linearly, the generalized least squares (GLS) estimate follows from the two innovation sequences,
\[
\hat{\nu}_0 = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{N} v_k^{(0)} v_k^{(\nu)} / S_k}{\sum_{k=1}^{N} \left(v_k^{(\nu)}\right)^2 / S_k},
\]
where the artifact-inflated \(S_k\) down-weights aberrant beats. With baseline-corrected innovations \(v_k = v_k^{(0)} - \hat{\nu}_0 v_k^{(\nu)}\) and \(\mathcal{K} = \{k : \mu_k < 100\}\) (all beats if fewer than two satisfy this), the concentrated estimate of the global scale and the profiled log-likelihood are
\[
\hat{\sigma}^2_{sys} = \frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{eff}}}\sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}}\frac{v_k^2}{S_k}, \qquad
\mathcal{L}^* = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}}\ln S_k - \frac{n_{\mathrm{eff}}}{2}\ln\hat{\sigma}^2_{sys}, \qquad n_{\mathrm{eff}} = |\mathcal{K}|.
\]
If \(\hat{\nu}_0\) is not finite and positive, the implied RR would be undefined, and the fit is assigned \(\mathcal{L}^* = -\infty\).
The reconstructed (forward-filtered) states are \(\hat{X}_{k|k} = \tilde{X}^{(0)}_{k|k} - \hat{\nu}_0\,\tilde{X}^{(\nu)}_{k|k}\). The variances of the drives include the uncertainty in \(\hat{\nu}_0\), whose variance is \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}/D\) with \(D = \sum_k (v^{(\nu)}_k)^2/S_k\):
\[
\mathrm{Var}(\hat{x}_{b,k}) = \hat{\sigma}^2_{sys}\left[P^{(bb)}_{k|k} + \frac{\left(\tilde{X}^{(\nu)}_{b,k|k}\right)^2}{D}\right], \quad b \in \{p, s\}.
\]
The filtered RR at beat \(k\) is \(\widehat{RR}_k = (1 + \hat{I}_{p,k} - \hat{I}_{s,k})/\hat{\nu}_0\) with variance \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\left(P^{(33)}_{k|k} + P^{(44)}_{k|k} - 2P^{(34)}_{k|k}\right)/\hat{\nu}_0^2\). Because these quantities use the update at beat \(k\), they are in-sample filtered values. The stated 95% intervals are conditional on the MAP kinetic parameters.

title: Supplementary material
text:
2.4 Spectral anchoring
The relative vagal variance \(\lambda_P = V_p/V_s\) is computed once per recording as follows.

Resampling. The instantaneous heart rate (Hz), \(1/\Delta t_k\), is interpolated onto a uniform 4 Hz grid with a monotone (Fritsch–Carlson) Hermite spline, which avoids overshoot between beats, and the mean is subtracted.
Global wavelet spectrum. A Morlet continuous wavelet transform is computed [R package biwavelet]. Power at each scale is masked outside the cone of influence and averaged over time to give the global spectrum \(G(f)\), and frequencies are sorted in ascending order.
Frequency weights. A logistic transition \(L(f) = \left[1 + \exp\{-s\,(f - f_c)\}\right]^{-1}\) with crossover \(f_c = 0.10\) Hz defines the weights \[
w_v(f) = \phi + (1 - \phi)\,L(f), \qquad w_s(f) = (1-\phi)\,\left(1 - L(f)\right),
\] with \(w_v + w_s = 1\), where \(\phi = 0.25\) is the floor fraction of the vagal weight at low frequencies. The steepness \(s = -\ln\{\epsilon/(1-\epsilon)\}/(f_u - f_c)\) is set so that \(1 - L(f_u) = \epsilon = 0.05\) at the LF/HF boundary \(f_u = 0.15\) Hz, which defines the “sympathetic leakage” into the high-frequency band.
Energy ratio. Energies are integrated by the trapezoidal rule over the log-spaced scales on \(0.04 \le f \le 0.40\) Hz, \[
E_v = \int w_v(f)\,G(f)\,df, \qquad E_s = \int w_s(f)\,G(f)\,df, \qquad \lambda_P = E_v/E_s .
\]

The unweighted low- and high-frequency band powers (LF: 0.04–0.15 Hz; HF: 0.15–0.40 Hz) and the mean heart rate are also stored as diagnostics and are not used in the fit.
The anchor rests on two assumptions that merit explicit statement. First, the spectral weights encode external evidence about the distribution of vagal and sympathetic modulation across frequency. Pharmacological blockade paradigms indicate that parasympathetic tone forms a persistent baseline contribution to resting LF power [1,2]; because the size of this contribution varies across individuals and conditions, the floor fraction is set to a deliberately conservative \(\phi\) = 0.25 (a quarter of the low-frequency weight is attributed to the vagal branch) and is varied between 0.10 and 0.50 in the sensitivity analyses. In addition, sympathetic oscillations peak heavily around the 0.10 Hz baroreflex resonance frequency (\(f_c\) = 0.10 Hz) [2]. Furthermore, due to the sluggish intracellular signaling kinetics of beta-adrenergic cascades, sympathetic transfer is structurally limited to a negligible leakage fraction of less than 5% (\(\epsilon\) = 0.05) above the standard 0.15 Hz high-frequency boundary [3–5]. Second, the OU drives have Lorentzian power spectra whose integral equals the stationary variance (Parseval relation), so that the ratio of partitioned energies in the observed heart-rate spectrum is taken as the ratio of latent stationary variances. This ignores differences in the transfer from latent drive to observed heart rate (for example, the low-pass effect of integration over each interval) and is therefore an approximation.

title: Supplementary material
text:
2.5 Priors, MAP objective and optimization
The parameters \(\theta = (\theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3)\) are mapped to the physical scale by \(\kappa_s = e^{\theta_1}\), \(\kappa_p = \kappa_s + e^{\theta_2}\) and \(\lambda_R = e^{\theta_3}\), which ensures positivity and \(\kappa_p > \kappa_s\) without bound constraints. The log-prior terms, defined up to additive constants, are as follows.
Time-scale priors. For \(b \in \{p, s\}\) with default central \(c\)-coverage interval \([\tau^{lo}_b, \tau^{hi}_b]\) (default \(c = 0.95\)),
\[
\ln p(\tau_b) = -\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\frac{\ln\tau_b - \mu_b}{\varsigma_b}\right)^2, \quad
\mu_b = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\ln\tau^{lo}_b + \ln\tau^{hi}_b\right), \quad
\varsigma_b = \frac{\ln\tau^{hi}_b - \ln\tau^{lo}_b}{2\,z_{(1+c)/2}},
\] that is, a log-normal prior whose central interval is the stated range, with \(z_{(1+c)/2}\) the standard normal quantile.
Separation prior. With \(U = (\kappa_p - \kappa_s)/(\kappa_p + \kappa_s) \in (0, 1)\) and \(1 - U = 2\kappa_s/(\kappa_p + \kappa_s)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ln p(U) &= (\alpha - 1)\ln U + (\beta - 1)\ln(1 - U), \\
\alpha - 1 &= w\,U^*, \quad \beta - 1 = w\,(1 - U^*), \quad U^* = \frac{r - 1}{r + 1},
\end{aligned}
\] which is a Beta density with mode \(U^*\) corresponding to \(\kappa_p/\kappa_s = r\) and strength \(w\). The defaults are \(r = 20\) and \(w = 10\).
Timing-jitter prior. The equivalent RR timing jitter at the median interval \(\tilde{\Delta t}\) is \(s_{RR} = \sqrt{\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\,\lambda_R\,\tilde{\Delta t}}/\hat\nu_0\), and a log-normal prior is placed on it, constructed as above from the central interval \([0.5, 20]\) ms. The hyperparameters are fixed and independent of the data, but \(s_{RR}\) depends on the profiled quantities.
The objective minimized is
\[
\mathrm{Cost}(\theta) = -\left[\mathcal{L}^* + \ln p(\tau_s) + \ln p(\tau_p) + \ln p(U) + \ln p(s_{RR})\right],
\] and non-finite values are replaced by \(10^{12}\) so that the optimizer backs off. Optimization uses the BFGS algorithm (R optim, finite-difference gradients, at most 1000 iterations) from a single start: \(\kappa_s\) and \(\kappa_p\) at the inverse of the geometric centers of the time-scale priors (with \(\kappa_p - \kappa_s\) floored at 0.05 s\(^{-1}\)), and \(\lambda_{R,0} = 10^{-3}\). A single start does not guarantee a global optimum.

title: Supplementary material
text:
2.6 Parameter uncertainty
Standard errors are computed from the numerical Hessian \(\mathcal{H}\) of \(\mathrm{Cost}(\theta)\) at the optimum. The covariance of \(\theta\) is approximated by the Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse \(\mathcal{H}^{+}\), which tolerates near-singularity, and mapped to the physical parameters through the Jacobian \(\mathcal{J}\) of \(\theta \mapsto (\kappa_s, \kappa_p, \lambda_R)\), giving \(\mathrm{Cov} = \mathcal{J}\,\mathcal{H}^{+}\,\mathcal{J}^\top\). For the time constants, the delta method gives \(\mathrm{Var}(\tau) \approx \mathrm{Var}(\kappa)/\kappa^4\). Wald 95% intervals are \(\text{estimate} \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}\). The profiled (\(\hat\nu_0\), \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\)), fixed (\(\lambda_P\), hyperparameters) and derived quantities carry no standard error, and the intervals therefore do not reflect uncertainty in \(\lambda_P\) or in the hyperparameters.

title: Supplementary material
text:
3.1 The classical Poisson arrival formulation
In classical point-process statistics, a heartbeat is a stochastic arrival governed by a conditional intensity function \(\lambda(t)\). The time-rescaling theorem states that integrating the intensity over the observed inter-beat interval \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\),
\[
\Lambda_k = \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k} \lambda(t)\, dt,
\]
transforms the sequence of intervals into unit-rate exponential variates, \(\Lambda_k \sim \text{Exp}(1)\). The exponential CDF maps these to a uniform distribution:
\[
u_k = 1 - \exp(-\Lambda_k) \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1),
\]
which is evaluated with the KS test.

title: Supplementary material
text:
3.2 The phase-domain diffusion formulation
In SPARK, the event is triggered when the accumulated phase reaches a threshold of \(1\), and the stochasticity arises from the diffusion within the interval together with uncertainty about the latent drives. Over the observed interval, the filter predicts the phase from the past data and the baseline, and the innovation is
\[
v_k = v_k^{(0)} - \hat{\nu}_0\,v_k^{(\nu)} = 1 - \hat{\nu}_0\,\Delta t_k - H\,\hat{X}_{k|k-1},
\]
the difference between the observed unit phase and its one-step-ahead prediction. If the model and the parameters are correct, \(v_k\) is conditionally Gaussian with zero mean and variance \(\sigma^2_{sys} S_k\), where \(S_k = H P_{k|k-1} H^\top + R_k\) combines the prediction uncertainty of the integrated drives and the threshold noise. In contrast to the exponential variates of the Poisson formulation, the standardized innovation is therefore normal.

title: Supplementary material
section: 3.3 Standardization and the probability integral transform
text:
3.3 Standardization and the probability integral transform
The standardized innovation is
\[
z_k = \frac{v_k}{\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\,S_k}} \;\approx\; \mathcal{N}(0, 1),
\]
and the probability integral transform with the standard normal CDF gives
\[
u_k = \Phi(z_k) \;\approx\; \mathcal{U}(0, 1).
\]
Uniformity of \(u_k\) is assessed with the KS distance \(D\), and the approximate 5% critical value is \(1.36/\sqrt{N}\). Because \(\hat{\nu}_0\), \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\) and the kinetic parameters are estimated from the same series, the nominal critical value is approximate, and the test is conservative in this respect. Serial independence is assessed with the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) of \(z_k\) over 40 lags, with bounds at \(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{N}\). Diagnostics retain beats with finite innovations and artifact multiplier \(\mu_k < 1.5\), and the innovation variance used for standardization excludes the artifact inflation. The plug-in values used for \(\hat\nu_0\) and \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\) make the standardized innovations approximate.
The diagnostic follows the time-rescaling principle of isolating the model-standardized noise and mapping it to a uniform distribution, and it is not an application of the Poisson-specific theorem. Agreement with uniformity and serial independence is necessary for adequacy but does not establish it, since the diagnostics may have limited power against specific misspecifications, including the structure of the latent decomposition.

title: Supplementary material
section: 5.1 Explicit derivation of the transition matrix
text:
5.1 Explicit derivation of the transition matrix
The matrix exponential is evaluated from its Taylor series,
\[
\exp(A\,\Delta t_k) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(A\,\Delta t_k)^n}{n!} = I + A\,\Delta t_k + \frac{1}{2!} A^2 \Delta t_k^2 + \dots
\]
Given the block structure of \(A\), its powers follow a regular pattern. For any integer \(n \ge 1\),
\[
A^n = \begin{bmatrix}
(-\kappa_p)^n & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & (-\kappa_s)^n & 0 & 0 \\
(-\kappa_p)^{n-1} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
0 & (-\kappa_s)^{n-1} & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
For the top-left element, which governs \(x_p\), the series reduces to the scalar exponential:
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-\kappa_p \Delta t_k)^n}{n!} = e^{-\kappa_p \Delta t_k}.
\]
For the element in position \((3,1)\), which governs \(I_p\), the series starts at \(n = 1\), because the identity matrix has a zero in this position. Extracting a factor of \(-1/\kappa_p\) gives
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\Delta t_k^n}{n!} (-\kappa_p)^{n-1} = -\frac{1}{\kappa_p} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(-\kappa_p \Delta t_k)^n}{n!}.
\]
The right-hand sum is the Taylor series of \(e^{-\kappa_p \Delta t_k}\) minus its \(n = 0\) term, which equals \(1\), so that
\[
-\frac{1}{\kappa_p} \left( e^{-\kappa_p \Delta t_k} - 1 \right) = \frac{1 - e^{-\kappa_p \Delta t_k}}{\kappa_p}.
\]
Because the vagal and sympathetic pathways are decoupled in \(A\), the same reduction applies to the sympathetic parameters. The element in position \((2,2)\) is
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-\kappa_s \Delta t_k)^n}{n!} = e^{-\kappa_s \Delta t_k},
\]
and the element in position \((4,2)\) is
\[
-\frac{1}{\kappa_s} \left( e^{-\kappa_s \Delta t_k} - 1 \right) = \frac{1 - e^{-\kappa_s \Delta t_k}}{\kappa_s}.
\]
Finally, the right half of \(A^n\) is zero for all \(n \ge 1\), so the elements in positions \((3,3)\) and \((4,4)\) come only from the identity matrix and equal \(1\). Assembling these scalar solutions gives the closed-form transition matrix \(\Phi_k\), in which the accumulation of the integral states is evaluated analytically and without numerical integration over each interval.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
Highlights




RR alone may leave vagal-like and sympathetic-like drives ambiguous
A phase-domain state-space model filters irregular RR intervals in continuous time
Physiological priors and a spectral anchor restrict the set of latent solutions
Latent states are examined during tilt, across aging and in exercise recovery
How change is split between the two drives remains conditional on the anchor
Abstract
Cardiac autonomic regulation is observed only through beat-to-beat (RR) intervals, and separating their variability into parasympathetic-like and sympathetic-like components is an inverse problem that RR alone is not expected to solve uniquely. We introduce SPARK (Stochastic Phase-domain Autonomic Reconstruction Kinetics), a physiology-informed stochastic state-space framework in which two independent Ornstein–Uhlenbeck drives modulate sinoatrial pacing through an integrate-and-fire phase. Conditioning on each observed interval yields a conditionally linear-Gaussian measurement equation and exact continuous-time filtering across irregular intervals. Time-scale priors, a kinetic ordering constraint and a wavelet-derived spectral partition restrict the admissible latent solutions. Across recordings, multi-start fits reached a median of 23.5 distinct solutions per recording without physiological information versus 1.0 with it, and one process absorbed essentially all variability in 75% versus 4% of the fits; the innovation diagnostics showed residual structure in most recordings (KS distance below its critical value in 22%). Reconstructions were then examined: in 10 tilt-table recordings, the vagal-like state decreased and the sympathetic-like state increased in 10 of 10; between 20 young and 20 older adults, 8 of 11 partly redundant latent summaries reached \(|\delta| \geq 0.33\); and in 263 exercise recordings, median recovery times, which are closely tied to the fitted time constants, were 41 s (vagal-like) and 336 s (sympathetic-like). SPARK offers a model-conditional description of autonomic trajectories complementing conventional heart rate variability; the split of a stressor-induced change between the drives remained sensitive to the spectral anchor, and latent states are reconstructions, not measurements of neural activity.
Keywords: Stochastic dynamics, State-space estimation, Identifiability, Autonomic nervous system, Heart rate variability, Integrate-and-fire

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.1 Conceptual model
SPARK represents the sinoatrial node as an integrate-and-fire pacemaker whose net drift is modulated by two latent autonomic drives. Let \(\phi(t)\) denote the sinoatrial phase, which is set to zero after each heartbeat and evolves as a drift–diffusion process,
\[
d\phi(t) = \nu(t)\,dt + \sigma_z\,dW(t), \qquad \nu(t) = \nu_0 - x_p(t) + x_s(t),
\]
where a beat occurs when \(\phi\) reaches a normalized threshold of \(1\) [14]. The net drift \(\nu(t)\) is the instantaneous pacing rate (Hz), \(\nu_0\) is an intrinsic baseline rate, \(\sigma_z\) is the diffusion coefficient of threshold-level noise, and \(x_p(t)\) and \(x_s(t)\) are latent parasympathetic-like and sympathetic-like drives, expressed in Hz as deviations from their homeostatic baseline. Hereafter we refer to them as the vagal and sympathetic drives for brevity. These labels denote the model components that are distinguished by their kinetics and spectral allocation (see Identification structure); they do not denote directly measured neural activity.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.2 Latent autonomic dynamics
The drives are independent, mean-reverting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) processes [27], which represent the tendency of each branch to return to its homeostatic level after a transient stimulus:
\[
\begin{aligned}
dx_p(t) &= -\kappa_p x_p(t)\,dt + \sigma_p\,dW_p(t),\\
dx_s(t) &= -\kappa_s x_s(t)\,dt + \sigma_s\,dW_s(t),
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(\kappa_p\) and \(\kappa_s\) are clearance rates (s\(^{-1}\)) with e-folding times \(\tau_p = 1/\kappa_p\) and \(\tau_s = 1/\kappa_s\). To keep amplitude independent of kinetics, the diffusion coefficients are parameterized through the stationary variances, \(\sigma_b = \sqrt{2\kappa_b V_b}\), with \(V_s = \sigma^2_{sys}\) and \(V_p = \lambda_P\,\sigma^2_{sys}\); \(\lambda_P = V_p/V_s\) is the relative vagal-to-sympathetic variance, and the global scale \(\sigma^2_{sys}\) factors out of the Kalman gain and can be profiled analytically. To make the observation equation linear, the state is augmented with the running integrals of the drives, \(dI_p = x_p\,dt\) and \(dI_s = x_s\,dt\), giving \(\tilde{X}(t) = [x_p, x_s, I_p, I_s]^\top\) and \(d\tilde{X} = A\,\tilde{X}\,dt + G\,dW\) with constant matrices \(A\) and \(G\). The transition over any observed interval \(\Delta t_k\) is then exact, \(\Phi_k = \exp(A\,\Delta t_k)\), with a closed-form process covariance (see the “Matrix exponential” and “Estimation algorithm” sections of the supplementary material, which also list the model quantities and their estimation status).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.3 Observation model: phase-domain inversion
In the strict first-passage formulation, the observed interval is the random time \(T = \inf\{t > 0 : \phi(t) \ge 1\}\), whose distribution is inverse Gaussian for a constant drift [15]; estimating a time-varying drift from it within a state-space model is a nonlinear problem [7,17]. We instead condition on the observed interval: the recorded duration \(\Delta t_k\) is a fixed window, and under a terminal-threshold condition the phase accumulated over \([t_{k-1}, t_k]\) equals one,
\[
1 = \nu_0\,\Delta t_k - \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k} x_p(t)\,dt + \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k} x_s(t)\,dt + v_k ,
\]
where \(v_k\) collects the Gaussian threshold-level noise, with variance \(\sigma_z^2\,\Delta t_k\) and \(\sigma_z^2 = \sigma^2_{sys}\lambda_R\). This neglects paths that cross the threshold and return below it within one interval, which is accurate when the drift is large relative to the noise (an explicit bound is given in the “Asymptotic convergence” section of the supplementary material). In the augmented state the observation is linear,
\[
1 - \nu_0\,\Delta t_k = H\,\tilde{X}_k + v_k, \qquad H = [0,\ 0,\ -1,\ 1],
\]
so standard Kalman recursions apply. After each measurement update the integral states and their covariances are reset to zero, whereas \(x_p\) and \(x_s\) continue to evolve, which represents the restart of phase accumulation at each beat while preserving the trans-beat memory of the drives. To limit the influence of ectopic beats and detection artifacts, the threshold-noise variance at beat \(k\) is inflated by a multiplier that grows with the largest relative change between adjacent intervals, which removes abrupt jumps from the likelihood without interrupting the propagation of the drives. The multiplier uses both neighbors and is therefore not strictly causal; it affects only the weighting of the observation. It is a heuristic robustness device and not a model of arrhythmia, so recordings with substantial non-sinus activity are outside the intended scope of the framework.

Structural constraints. Exponential links ensure positive rates, and \(\kappa_p = \kappa_s + \exp(\theta_2)\) imposes \(\kappa_p > \kappa_s\), which removes the label-switching permutation between the two drives.
Time-scale information. Independent log-normal priors on \(\tau_p\) and \(\tau_s\), and a Beta prior on \(U\) that discourages the two time scales from collapsing onto one another, reflect the expected separation between rapid vagal and slow sympathetic effector kinetics [2,20]. The limits for \(\tau_p\) align with rapid parasympathetic signaling and respiratory cycles, and those for \(\tau_s\) with the inertia and low-pass behavior of sympathetic modulation [20,22,28]. The priors are fixed across recordings and not derived from the individual series.
Spectral information. The ratio \(\lambda_P\) is a deterministic function of the global wavelet spectrum of the heart rate [29,30], which is partitioned into vagal and sympathetic energy with logistic frequency weights: sympathetic weight dominates at low frequencies, vagal weight rises at a crossover of 0.10 Hz, sympathetic weight falls to 5% at the LF/HF boundary of 0.15 Hz, and the vagal branch keeps a floor fraction of the low-frequency weight to reflect its contribution under non-stationarity. The weights encode external evidence on how modulation by the two branches is distributed across frequency, including pharmacological-blockade studies [21–23,31,32]. Because \(\lambda_P\) is computed from the series being fitted, it is data-informed but not independent of the data; the physiological information resides in the weighting function, and equating the ratio of spectral energies with the ratio of latent variances is an approximation (“Spectral anchoring” section of the supplementary material).
A prior on the equivalent RR timing jitter, with a 95% interval of 0.5–20 ms, spans the range expected for electrocardiographic and photoplethysmographic acquisition. These specifications are model assumptions informed by external evidence; they are not estimated from the present data, and their influence on the inferred trajectories is evaluated in the identifiability analyses described below.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.5 Inference and uncertainty
For a given parameter vector, the Kalman recursion (with the Joseph form of the covariance update) processes the observed intervals sequentially. The baseline \(\nu_0\) enters the observation equation linearly and, together with the global scale \(\sigma^2_{sys}\), is profiled out analytically by generalized least squares, using two filters that share a single Kalman gain; the profiled log-likelihood is computed over the beats with an artifact multiplier below 100. The remaining parameters \(\theta = (\ln\kappa_s,\ \ln(\kappa_p - \kappa_s),\ \ln\lambda_R)\) are estimated by minimizing the negative log-posterior, that is, the negative profiled log-likelihood plus the negative log-prior terms of Table 1, with BFGS from a single start at the centers of the time-scale priors. The reconstructed states are the forward-filtered (causal) estimates, and the reported 95% intervals for the states and for the filtered RR are conditional on the MAP kinetic parameters and do not incorporate uncertainty in those parameters. Standard errors for \(\kappa_p\), \(\kappa_s\) and \(\lambda_R\) come from the numerical Hessian of the MAP objective and the delta method; profiled, fixed and derived quantities carry no standard error. Algorithmic details are given in the “Estimation algorithm” section of the supplementary material. The model was implemented in R, and a browser-based implementation with the same specification (default settings as in this study: \(M_3\), vagal floor 0.25) is available for single recordings (see Code availability).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.6 Model diagnostics
Fit and convergence. Convergence is defined by the optimizer return code. Filtered tracking accuracy is quantified by the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and the root mean square error (RMSE) between the observed and filtered implied RR; these are in-sample measures, because the implied RR at each beat uses states updated with that beat, and they are not out-of-sample prediction error.
Innovation diagnostics. The standardized innovations \(z_k = v_k/\sqrt{\hat\sigma^2_{sys}S_k}\) should be independent standard normal variates if the model is adequate. Following the time-rescaling principle, \(u_k = \Phi(z_k)\) was tested against the uniform distribution with the Kolmogorov–Smirnov (KS) distance \(D\), which was compared with the approximate recording-specific critical value \(1.36/\sqrt{N}\) (approximate because the parameters are estimated from the same data; its behavior under a correctly specified model was examined by simulation). The distribution of \(D\) across recordings is reported instead of dichotomous \(p\)-value thresholds. Serial dependence was assessed with the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) of \(z_k\) over 40 lags, with bounds at \(\pm 1.96/\sqrt{N}\), using beats with an artifact multiplier below 1.5 (“Goodness-of-fit diagnostic” section of the supplementary material).

2.7 Identifiability analyses
Model specifications. To evaluate whether RR alone identifies the decomposition and whether physiological information reduces the ambiguity, four nested specifications were compared (Table 2). The specification \(M_3\), which combines all the physiological information, is used for the fit diagnostics and for the perturbation, aging and exercise analyses. All specifications retain the structural constraints of Table 1, so that the comparison does not include label switching between the two drives. In \(M_0\) and \(M_1\), \(\lambda_P\) is a free parameter, whereas in \(M_2\) and \(M_3\) it is fixed by the spectral anchor. title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.8 Data, preprocessing and event definition
Data and cleaning. Each recording is a table of ECG-derived RR intervals with their times and, when available, blood pressure, respiration (Fantasia) or the tilt-table angle (PRCP). RR intervals and covariates were cleaned with an adaptive running-median/median-absolute-deviation gate, chosen on simulated series with injected artifacts because it altered few artifact-free beats (about 0.2%) while correcting most artifacts (about 99.7%); analyses that use a covariate were restricted to recordings with at least 80% valid values in the analysis window. The latent model itself uses only the RR intervals. Preparation, cleaning and their checks are described in the “Data preparation and its checks” section of the supplementary material.
Participants. The PRCP database contains ten healthy adults (the database reports neither age nor sex). The Fantasia database contains 20 young (21–34 years) and 20 older (68–85 years) healthy adults, with equal numbers of men and women in each group as reported by the database; the sex of the participants is as recorded by the data source. The exercise cohort consists of community-dwelling adults aged 60 years or older from the Magallanes region of Chile, recruited for the study that produced these recordings, where the sample is described [33]; 263 recordings were analyzed. Sex and gender were not used as covariates in any analysis: the only subject characteristic analyzed was group membership in Fantasia.
Events. Every tilt and every stand-up of the PRCP protocol is an event analyzed separately against its own baseline. Onsets and returns were taken from the tilt-angle signal where available, from the protocol annotations otherwise, and, for recordings with neither and for the exercise recordings, from the heart-rate series itself: heart rate in 5-s bins was segmented into piecewise-constant levels, with the number of segments chosen by the Bayesian information criterion subject to a minimum difference of 0.10 Hz (about 6 bpm) between adjacent levels. Heart rate alone cannot tell a tilt from another maneuver that raises it, so such events are candidates and not confirmed tilts, and, because they are detected from the same RR series that is modeled, timing relative to them is not independent evidence about the states; the analyses therefore emphasize the relative timing and amplitude of the two components. The algorithms and their accuracy are given in the “Event detection” section of the supplementary material.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.9 Validation framework: orthostatic perturbation
The first biological test of the reconstructed states uses tilt-table recordings from the Physiologic Response to Changes in Posture (PRCP) dataset [34]. The aim is to assess whether the inferred components change in the expected direction during a perturbation, not to establish that either component is parasympathetic or sympathetic. Expected responses, based on the physiology of orthostatic stress, are a reduction of the vagal drive soon after the perturbation onset and a slower, more sustained increase of the sympathetic drive. Each maneuver was analyzed against its own baseline (60 to 180 s, beginning 120 s after the previous maneuver returned), followed by the maneuver itself and a 120-s recovery window. We computed (i) the difference in the mean of each state between phases, standardized by the baseline SD of that state; (ii) whether each difference had the expected sign; and (iii) a step-response fit of each state, \(x(t) = x_0 + D\,[1 - e^{-(t-t_0)/\tau}]\) for \(t \ge t_0\), yielding the response latency, the time constant and the relative onset lag \(t_{0,s} - t_{0,p}\) (fits at the search bounds are flagged). Between-recording summaries used one value per recording, the median over its tilts, so that a recording with more tilts did not weigh more; the share of individual tilts with the expected pattern is reported as a measure of within-recording consistency. As a negative control, the same contrast was computed between the two halves of the resting baseline of each tilt, where no perturbation separates them, and compared with the tilt contrast (shares with exact 95% intervals and a paired signed-rank test of the absolute standardized changes over recordings; definition in the supplementary material). Reconstructions are displayed as time series with 95% intervals, as averages of tilts aligned on the onset (each relative to its own baseline) and as trajectories in the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane in units of the baseline SDs. Secondary analyses (temporal resolution against a CWT moving spectrum, the arterial-pressure response and its lagged correlation with the states, the dose–response over tilt angle, and the responses by kind of maneuver) are described and reported in the “Secondary analyses of the perturbation” section of the supplementary material.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.10 Generalization: aging
To examine whether the representation differs between young and older adults, we analyzed resting recordings from the Fantasia database [35], using only membership of the young or older group (taken from the record names) and a fixed analysis window (600 s starting at 600 s of the recording); no further covariates, such as continuous age or sex, were available. The question is which dimensions of the model-based description differ between groups, and not whether any single parameter is associated with age: the intrinsic rate \(\nu_0\), the time constants \(\tau_p\) and \(\tau_s\), the log-ratio \(\ln(\kappa_p/\kappa_s)\), the relative vagal variance \(\lambda_P\), the global scale \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\), the equivalent timing jitter, the SD of each reconstructed state and their ratio, and the share of \(x_p\) variance. Group differences (older minus young) are summarized by the Hodges–Lehmann shift, the Wilcoxon rank-sum \(p\)-value and Cliff’s \(\delta\) with a percentile bootstrap interval, with Benjamini–Hochberg control within each family of variables (latent and conventional HRV). Because the kinetic estimates are shaped by informative priors, group differences in \(\tau\) are interpreted relative to those priors. Stability was examined by refitting two non-overlapping windows of each recording and by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC(3,1)) of the log-transformed values. With the group sizes available, all tests are exploratory. The respiratory and blood-pressure analyses of the same recordings are described and reported in the “Additional analyses of the Fantasia recordings” section of the supplementary material.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.11 Exercise and recovery
The functional demonstration uses a two-minute step test with a rest–exercise–rest protocol in older adults [33]. Each recording is fitted individually, with time-invariant kinetic parameters, and the non-stationary exercise response is represented by the time-varying filtered states. The rest level of each state is its mean (and SD) from 20 s after the start to 5 s before the detected onset; the exercise response is the difference between the mean of the state over the last 15 s of exercise and the rest level (also expressed in rest SDs), together with the peak excursion; and the geometry of the \((x_p, x_s)\) path, in units of the rest SDs, is summarized by its length, the area it encloses and the maximum distance from the rest point. No clinical or functional outcome measures and no subject characteristics were available for this cohort, and therefore no analyses of association with such variables are performed.
Recovery time. Because no single definition of recovery is canonical, four candidate definitions and three rules for the end of exercise were compared on simulated rest–exercise–recovery recordings with known recovery constants and end times, and the best-scoring combination was used; recordings that did not meet the criterion within the observation window were treated as right-censored (Kaplan–Meier medians are reported). The benchmark depends on the simulated profiles and is therefore a methodological check of the definitions, and not evidence about the real recordings (“Recovery-time benchmark” section of the supplementary material).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.12 Conventional HRV comparators
Conventional HRV measures (SDNN, RMSSD, mean heart rate, and LF and HF power from a tapered periodogram of the resampled tachogram, the latter only for windows of at least 120 s) are used as comparators and not as competitors. The question is whether the latent representation provides information that is not directly encoded by these descriptors, examined descriptively through rank correlations between latent summaries and HRV metrics within each dataset and, in the perturbation and exercise recordings, through the relation of phase-specific HRV metrics to the corresponding latent responses. Leave-one-out analyses of how well HRV metrics predict the latent summaries, and of group discrimination in Fantasia, are described in the “Additional analyses of the Fantasia recordings” section of the supplementary material.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
2.13 Statistical reporting
Quantities that vary across recordings are summarized as the median and the 2.5th–97.5th percentile range across recordings. This range describes between-recording dispersion; it is not a confidence interval for the median. Proportions are given with exact (Clopper–Pearson) 95% intervals; they are descriptive, since the tilts of one recording are not independent. None of the analyses was preregistered, and those on the PRCP, Fantasia and exercise recordings are exploratory. Fixed random seeds are used throughout, and the analysis code, configuration and session information are provided with the supplementary material.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
section: 3.1 RR alone did not uniquely determine the latent decomposition in these data
text:
3.1 RR alone did not uniquely determine the latent decomposition in these data
We first asked whether the RR series alone is sufficient to identify the latent vagal and sympathetic drives. To address this, the model was fitted without physiological information (\(M_0\)) from dispersed starting values, and the resulting parameter estimates, likelihood values and reconstructed trajectories were compared across starts, in a subset of 150 recordings drawn from the three datasets. Evidence for under-determination would consist of solutions with comparable fit to RR but different latent decompositions, including solutions in which one process absorbs essentially all variability.
Without physiological information (\(M_0\); 150 recordings), the multi-start fits of a recording reached a median of 23.5 distinct solutions per recording and 60.0 fits within 2 log-likelihood units of the best; among those, the SD of \(\ln\tau_s\) was 0.01, the share of \(x_p\) variance spanned a range of 0.00, and one process absorbed essentially all variability in 75% of the fits. Under the full specification (\(M_3\)), the corresponding values were: a median of 1.0 distinct solutions per recording and 100.0 fits within 2 log-likelihood units of the best; among those, the SD of \(\ln\tau_s\) was 0.00, the share of \(x_p\) variance spanned a range of 0.00, and one process absorbed essentially all variability in 4% of the fits. The number of distinct solutions per recording under \(M_3\) was lower than that under \(M_0\) (median 1.0 versus 23.5), and one process absorbed essentially all variability in 4% versus 75% of the fits. The dispersion of \(\ln\tau_s\) among near-equivalent fits under \(M_3\) was lower than that under \(M_0\) (larger under \(M_0\) in 3 of 3 datasets: exercise, fantasia and prcp); it was small under both specifications, so the contrast rests mainly on the number of distinct solutions and on one-process solutions. The best RR error under \(M_3\) was higher than that under \(M_0\) (median 3.39 versus 1.00 ms; a factor of 3.4, small in absolute terms but not in relative terms). In these recordings, the RR series alone therefore left the latent decomposition less well determined than the constrained specification, consistent with the premise that physiological information is needed to restrict the admissible solutions. This shows that the constraints reduce the ambiguity; it does not show that the retained solution is the correct decomposition. The median SD of \(\ln\tau_s\) among near-equivalent fits was 0.01 for \(M_0\), 0.00 for \(M_1\), 2.83 for \(M_2\), 0.00 for \(M_3\) (lowest under \(M_3\)). The best RR error differed by at most 2.40 ms (240%) between specifications, and the share of fits with both time constants inside the 95% prior intervals was 4% for \(M_0\) and 18% for \(M_3\). One process absorbed essentially all variability in 75% under \(M_0\), 83% under \(M_1\), 23% under \(M_2\) and 4% under \(M_3\) of the fits. Time-scale priors alone (\(M_1\)) therefore did not prevent one-process solutions, whereas the specifications that include the spectral anchor (\(M_2\), \(M_3\)) largely did; the lower ambiguity under \(M_3\) thus comes largely from fixing the variance ratio of the two drives through the anchor, and it should not be read as evidence that the apportionment between the drives is correct. The \(M_3\) estimates lay inside the 95% prior interval in 19% (\(\tau_p\)) and 97% (\(\tau_s\)) of recordings, with a median posterior contraction of 0.59 and 0.57 for \(\ln\tau_p\) and \(\ln\tau_s\), respectively. For the vagal-like drive, most estimates therefore lay outside the 95% prior interval, so the data moved \(\tau_p\) away from the central region of its prior; this may reflect slower fluctuations being absorbed by the faster drive, and it limits the reading of \(\tau_p\) as a strictly vagal time constant. In simulations with known truth, when the true time constants lay outside the prior intervals, the median absolute log-error of \(\tau_s\) was 1.32 for \(M_0\) and 0.98 for \(M_3\) (the \(M_3\) error was lower than the \(M_0\) error); when they lay inside, 1.40 and 0.19. These values delimit the claim: constraints that help when the truth is compatible with them can bias the estimates when it is not. The 95% intervals of the filtered \(M_3\) states, which are conditional on the MAP parameters, contained the true state at 70% to 100% of the time points across the four scenarios; the lowest coverage was that of \(x_s\) in the sympathetic-dominant variance scenario (70%).
For \(M_3\), optimization converged for 313 of 313 recordings (100.0%), and the following summaries refer to the converged fits (exercise (n = 263), fantasia (n = 40), prcp (n = 10)). The filtered reconstruction of RR had a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 0.213% [0.003, 5.544] and an RMSE of 2.503 ms [0.025, 89.252] (median [2.5th, 97.5th percentile] across recordings); because the implied RR at each beat uses states updated with that beat, these values describe in-sample filtered fit and not predictive accuracy. The innovation diagnostics indicate that the assumptions of serially independent, Gaussian innovations are met only partly in the recordings: the KS distance had a median of \(D\) = 0.056 [0.023, 0.172] against a mean recording-specific critical value of 0.0376 (approximate, because the parameters are estimated from the same data), \(D\) was below its critical value in 21.7% of recordings, compared with 0% exceeding it in well-specified simulations, and the innovation PACF departs from white noise (12.9 lags outside the approximate bounds on average; Supplementary Figure S10). Residual structure of this kind plausibly reflects components that the model does not represent, for example respiratory and baroreflex oscillations, and the reconstructed states should be read as conditional on this misspecification.
The estimated clearance rates were 0.07 s\(^{-1}\) [0.02, 0.74] for the vagal drive, corresponding to an e-folding time of 13.65 s [1.36, 44.17], and 0.007 s\(^{-1}\) [0.005, 0.010] for the sympathetic drive, corresponding to 149.1 s [99.2, 219.6] (Supplementary Figure S10, panel D). These estimates should be interpreted as MAP estimates under informative physiological priors and an enforced ordering \(\kappa_p > \kappa_s\). The separation of the two time scales is therefore a property of the identification structure and the data jointly, and does not by itself constitute independent evidence that the two drives have been segregated “blindly”. The extent to which the data move the estimates away from the prior centers is quantified by the contraction and prior-contrast values reported above.
Having examined whether physiological information reduces ambiguity, we next asked whether the resulting states exhibit expected responses to an independently characterized perturbation.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
3.3 Latent states during orthostatic perturbation
For the PRCP recordings, the tilts were taken from the tilt-angle signal where available (10 of 10 recordings) and from the protocol annotations otherwise. Each recording contained several maneuvers (40 tilts and 20 stand-ups analyzed in total). The filtered states of one recording are shown in Figure 2 (panel A) together with heart rate, arterial pressure and tilt angle, and the average response to a tilt in panel B; whether the components follow the expected pattern across recordings is summarized below, as a test of physiological coherence and should not be treated as proof that they correspond to the activity of the respective autonomic branches.






Figure 2: Latent states during repeated orthostatic perturbation. (A) One recording (recording 12734, median standardized response): filtered drives (blue, vagal-like \(x_p\); red, sympathetic-like \(x_s\)) with 95% intervals conditional on the MAP parameters, heart rate, mean arterial pressure and tilt angle; each tilt is shaded and numbered, and each stand-up (green) is labeled S. (B) All tilts aligned on their onset, each relative to its own baseline (states in baseline SDs; heart rate and MAP as changes); the line is the median over recordings, the band the quartiles and the grey lines the individual recordings. (C) Median path of the two states in the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane in baseline SDs. (D) Standardized change of the two states between baseline and tilt (large points: recordings; small points: individual tilts); changes of \(x_s\) reach tens of baseline SDs because the baseline SD of \(x_s\) is small. (E) Onset of the response of each state, and of MAP when available, relative to the tilt onset (open symbols: at a search bound). (F) Step-response time constants. (G) Peak lagged correlation between each state and MAP after detrending, with its lag (the sign differs between recordings, so it is not a consistent coupling). When recordings with several tilt-angle levels are available, a further panel shows the mean states, heart rate and MAP by angle. The accuracy of the heart-rate-based events is shown in Supplementary Figure S5.



In 10 recordings with a defined perturbation (40 tilts, each analyzed against its own baseline; a recording contributes the median over its tilts), the vagal-like state decreased and the sympathetic-like state increased in 10 of 10 (exact 95% interval 69% to 100%), which is consistent with the expected pattern of vagal withdrawal with sympathetic engagement. The same pattern was present in 98% of the individual tilts. As a negative control, the same contrast applied to the two halves of each tilt’s resting baseline gave the expected pattern in 14 of 40 baselines (35%; exact 95% interval 21% to 52%), against 39 of 40 tilts (98%; 87% to 100%), so the pattern is clearly less frequent without a perturbation; the median absolute standardized change was 7.5 times larger for \(x_p\) and 9.6 times larger for \(x_s\) during the tilt (exact paired signed-rank test over 10 recordings, one-sided: \(p < 0.001\) for both). A placebo share above the 25% expected for two independent random signs suggests slow drift within the baseline. Because heart rate rises during tilt, the net change of the two states is largely fixed by RR; what the spectral anchor and the priors determine is how that change is apportioned between the two drives. The sympathetic-like response began a median of 11.0 s after the vagal-like response, and its time constant was higher than that of the vagal-like response (80.7 versus 3.8 s); 70% of the \(x_p\) and 40% of the \(x_s\) step-response fits reached a search bound, so these constants are approximate. With 10 recordings and with events partly defined from the same RR series, this is a test of physiological coherence and not evidence that the components correspond to the activity of the respective autonomic branches.
The reconstructed dynamics of one recording, the average response and the group-level summaries are shown in Figure 2. Responses by kind of maneuver (slow tilt, rapid tilt, stand-up), the arterial-pressure response and its lagged correlation with the states, the dose–response over tilt angle and the comparison with a CWT moving spectrum are reported in the supplementary material (sections “Secondary analyses of the perturbation” and “Responses by type of maneuver”).
We then asked whether the representation is stable across individuals and whether it differs between young and older adults.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
section: 3.4 The latent representation across healthy aging
text:
3.4 The latent representation across healthy aging
The aging analysis addresses which dimensions of the model-based description differ between young and older adults in the Fantasia database, and not simply whether a given parameter differs. Only group membership was available as a subject characteristic: the analysis comprised 20 young and 20 older adults.
Among 20 young and 20 older adults, 8 of 11 latent variables reached \(|\delta| \geq 0.33\): \(\tau_p\) (higher in older adults, \(\delta\) = 0.72; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), \(\lambda_P\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.53; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), \(\hat\sigma^2_{sys}\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.71; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), the SD of \(x_p\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.81; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), the SD of \(x_s\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.61; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), the SD ratio \(x_p/x_s\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.54; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)), \(\ln(\kappa_p/\kappa_s)\) (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.69; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)) and the share of \(x_p\) variance (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.54; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)); 2 of 4 HRV variables reached \(|\delta| \geq 0.33\): SDNN (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.71; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)) and RMSSD (lower in older adults, \(\delta\) = -0.81; adjusted \(p < 0.05\)). These latent summaries are not independent: the share of \(x_p\) variance is a monotone function of the SD ratio of the two states, both depend strongly on the spectral anchor \(\lambda_P\), \(\ln(\kappa_p/\kappa_s)\) combines the two time constants, and \(\sigma^2_{sys}\) and the SDs of the states scale with the overall amplitude of variability, so that the count above overstates the number of distinct dimensions in which the groups differ. Agreement between two non-overlapping windows of the same recording (ICC of the log values) had a median of 0.88 for the latent summaries and 0.93 for the conventional HRV metrics; the lowest agreement was that of \(\tau_s\) (0.31). With these group sizes, all comparisons are exploratory, and no continuous age, sex or other covariates were available. Group contrasts are shown in Figure 3 and listed in the “Additional analyses of the Fantasia recordings” section of the supplementary material, together with the respiration and blood-pressure measures.






Figure 3: Latent representation in young and older adults. (A) Distributions of latent summaries by group. (B) Effect sizes (Cliff’s \(\delta\), older versus young) for latent and conventional HRV variables. (C) Test-retest agreement (ICC(3,1) of log values) between two non-overlapping windows.



Finally, we asked whether the reconstructed trajectories characterize adaptation and recovery during exercise.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
section: 3.5 Latent dynamics during exercise and recovery
text:
3.5 Latent dynamics during exercise and recovery
In the two-minute step-test recordings, the reconstruction tracked the changes in RR across rest, exercise and recovery (Figure 4, panel A). The rest, exercise and recovery phases were identified from heart rate. The recovery definition (90% recovery of the excursion) and the end-of-exercise rule (offset time of the fitted exercise profile) were those selected by the simulation benchmark (supplementary figure S3).
In 263 of 263 exercise recordings the rest, exercise and recovery phases could be defined from heart rate. From rest to the end of exercise, the vagal-like state changed by -7.6 [-26.3, -1.3] and the sympathetic-like state by 24.9 [5.5, 59.5] rest SDs, with a heart-rate increase of 40 [19, 117] bpm (median [2.5th, 97.5th percentile] across recordings). Recovery times (90% recovery of the excursion; Kaplan-Meier medians) were 41 s for the vagal-like state (1% of recordings censored) and 336 s for the sympathetic-like state (36% of recordings censored). For a first-order relaxation, recovery to 90% of the excursion takes about \(2.3\,\tau\), so these times are of the order implied by the estimated time constants, which are themselves shaped by their priors; they describe the fitted kinetics and are not independent measurements of recovery. The path in the state plane had a median length of 218 [102, 590], an enclosed area of 213 [38, 1051] and a maximum energy \(U\) of 252 [36, 1525] in rest-SD units. In the state plane, the strongest basin of the occupied region (the mode of the density of the filtered states) was displaced from its position in the rest phase by 9.2 rest-SD units to the exercise phase and 2.3 rest-SD units to the recovery phase (Supplementary Figure S6); the number of basins detected was 1 in the rest phase, 3 in the exercise phase, 1 in the recovery phase. The landscape is a descriptive map of where the states lie and is not a fitted potential of the model. Conventional HRV metrics predicted the latent summaries of this cohort with a median leave-one-out \(R^2\) of 0.40. The strongest rank correlation between a latent response and an HRV change was -0.61 (standardized change of the vagal-like state with the change in SDNN, n = 263). No subject characteristics or clinical and functional outcomes were available for this cohort, so the analysis is descriptive and no association with such variables is reported. The corresponding example recording is shown in Figure 4.






Figure 4: Adaptation and recovery in older adults. (A) One recording (recording 179, median standardized response): filtered states and heart rate, with the detected exercise shaded. (B) All recordings aligned on the end of exercise, each relative to its rest level (median, bands of 25–75% and 10–90% of recordings, and the recording of A). (C) Recovery times of each state (open symbols: right-censored at the end of the recording; bars: Kaplan–Meier medians). (D) Filtered states in the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane in rest-SD units, one panel per phase on common axes (central 99% of the pooled points): density of the points of the phase (colored hexagons) over that of all phases (grey), ellipses holding 50% (solid) and 90% (dashed) of them, and the median path through the phase (arrow; open circle: start).



The occupation of the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane in each phase is summarized as a density in Supplementary Figure S6; this map is descriptive and is not a potential function estimated from the model.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
4.1 Principal observations
We examined whether a physiology-informed latent state-space model can reconstruct model-conditional autonomic dynamics from RR intervals when the latent decomposition is not guaranteed to be identified by the observations alone. The premise of the study is that a close fit to RR does not by itself guarantee a physiologically meaningful decomposition, so that independent physiological information is better treated as part of the identification structure than as an auxiliary refinement. In the recordings analyzed, adding the physiological information reduced the number of distinct latent solutions and the occurrence of one-process solutions relative to RR alone, at a cost in RR error. In the datasets analyzed, the innovation diagnostics indicated residual serial structure or a departure from the assumed innovation distribution in most recordings, so that the reconstructions are conditional on a noise model that holds only approximately; with this caveat, in the tilt-table, aging and exercise analyses, the vagal-like state decreased and the sympathetic-like state increased in most tilt-table recordings; most of the partly redundant latent summaries differed between young and older adults; and the exercise recordings showed a rest-exercise-recovery trajectory whose recovery times are closely tied to the fitted time constants. These findings concern the behavior of a model-based representation under stated assumptions and should not be taken as direct evidence about neural activity. The latent states have not been validated against an external measure of autonomic activity; the evidence is of internal consistency and of agreement with expected qualitative responses.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
section: 4.2 Physiological meaning of the latent trajectories
text:
4.2 Physiological meaning of the latent trajectories
The latent trajectories are physiologically constrained reconstructions. They describe the drives, endowed with the kinetic and spectral properties assumed in the identification structure, that would be required for the model to account for the observed interval timing. This is the sense in which the components are called vagal-like and sympathetic-like: their identity rests on the imposed kinetic ordering and spectral allocation and not on independent measurement. During orthostatic tilt, the reconstructed vagal-like state decreased and the sympathetic-like state increased in 10 of 10 recordings (100%), a pattern consistent with the expected autonomic adaptation to orthostatic stress. The same contrast was clearly less frequent in the resting baselines (negative control), where it reflects drift and not a perturbation. Representing adaptation as a trajectory in the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane, with summaries such as path length or enclosed area, offers a compact description of response and recovery. The quadratic energy \(U\) used for display is computed from the estimated stationary covariance and is a descriptive device. Interpreting trajectory loops in terms of dissipation, entropy production or allostatic load would require independent validation and is not supported by the present analyses.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
4.3 Relationship with conventional HRV
Conventional HRV metrics summarize the variability of the RR series and remain robust and widely understood descriptors of the output of the system. SPARK addresses a complementary question: rather than asking how variable RR is, it asks what latent dynamical state could account for how RR changes, and how that state responds, adapts and recovers. The two approaches are therefore descriptive and generative, respectively, and neither is intended to replace the other. Window-based spectral estimates trade temporal against frequency resolution under non-stationary conditions [5,11], whereas the filter updates beat by beat. A comparison with a CWT moving spectrum in the tilt recordings is given in the supplementary material (section “Secondary analyses of the perturbation”); the temporal behavior of the filter depends on its own assumptions, including independent drives and time-invariant kinetics within a recording, and does not establish general superiority. In the Fantasia recordings, HRV metrics predicted the latent summaries with a median leave-one-out \(R^2\) of 0.42, so that a substantial part of their variation was not linearly recoverable from SDNN, RMSSD and mean heart rate.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
4.4 Identification and physiological priors
In an underdetermined inverse problem, physiological knowledge is not merely an auxiliary source of prior information; it forms part of the identification structure of the model (Table 1): positivity and the ordering \(\kappa_p > \kappa_s\) are structural, the time-scale and separation priors restrict where kinetic solutions can lie, the spectral anchor allocates variance between the two drives, and the jitter prior limits the extent to which the noise term can absorb autonomic variability.
Two consequences follow from this design. First, the kinetic estimates are posterior modes under informative priors that are fixed across recordings. They are bounded by the assumed ranges, and differences between groups or conditions in \(\kappa\) should therefore be interpreted together with the contrast between prior and posterior. The separation of fast and slow time scales is built into the identification structure and is not, by itself, an empirical finding. Second, the spectral anchor assigns branch energy by frequency and is computed from the same recording. Conditions in which the two branches overlap in frequency, such as strong orthostatic stress or exercise, may violate the assumed allocation and lead to misattribution between the drives [8,36]. The pharmacological evidence on which the spectral weights are based was drawn from the literature and was not generated here. These assumptions are explicit, and their influence is evaluated through the identifiability and sensitivity analyses. Varying the physiological hyperparameters one at a time changed the time constants by a median absolute log-ratio of at most 0.66 and left the reconstructed trajectories correlated at least 0.99 with the reference. The direction and time course of the reconstructed states were therefore robust to these settings. Correlations are insensitive to a change of scale, however, and do not address how variance is apportioned between the two drives: the share of latent variance attributed to the vagal-like process changed by a median absolute 0.23 at most, for the vagal floor (0.5), and by 0.35 when the spectral anchor was removed, so statements about the split between the two drives are conditional on the anchor settings (see the limitations).

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
section: 4.5 Phase-domain formulation and relation to existing approaches
text:
4.5 Phase-domain formulation and relation to existing approaches
Point-process models of heartbeat intervals based on generalized linear structures are largely phenomenological with respect to the sinoatrial node [15,37], whereas state-space formulations of the integral pulse frequency modulation framework generally solve the nonlinear first-passage observation model in the time domain and rely on extended or unscented filtering [14,17,18]. By conditioning on the observed interval, SPARK obtains a Gaussian measurement equation that is linear in the integrated drives, together with exact propagation of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck dynamics across irregular intervals, which avoids discretization error in the transitions. The price is the terminal-threshold approximation: the neglected boundary-reflection term is bounded in proportion to the ratio of diffusion to the square root of the drift (see the supplementary material), which is small in the high-drift, low-noise regime but is not zero and should be examined in recordings with large threshold noise; in the fitted recordings, \(\varepsilon = s_{RR}/\Delta t\) had a median of 0.0062 (maximum 0.0579), corresponding to a bound of at most 0.0116 on the CDF discrepancy.
Under the strict first-passage formulation, the variance of the interval scales with the inverse cube of the drift, in qualitative agreement with the dependence of respiratory sinus arrhythmia on vagal tone (“Interval-variance scaling” section of the supplementary material). SPARK conditions on the observed interval and uses a Gaussian measurement equation whose variance does not depend on the vagal level, so this dependence is not represented and the stationary variances of the two drives are treated as constant within a recording.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
4.6 Relation to nonlinear stochastic dynamics
Seen as a dynamical system, SPARK couples a fast and a slow mean-reverting stochastic process to a threshold-crossing phase oscillator that is reset at every event, and the data are the crossing times. Three aspects connect it to general questions of nonlinear stochastic dynamics. First, the observation is a first-passage problem: conditioning on the observed interval replaces it by a terminal-threshold condition whose error is bounded and small in the fitted regime (see Phase-domain formulation), so that an intrinsically nonlinear observation becomes tractable by exact linear-Gaussian filtering while the hybrid continuous–discrete reset of the integral states is preserved. Second, identifiability is here a question about time-scale separation: the fitted rates of the two drives differ by a median factor of 11 in these recordings, and when the likelihood is left unconstrained it shows ridges along which solutions with very different time scales and variance partitions fit the intervals almost equally well (Section 3.1); an external anchor on how variance is distributed across frequency is what removes this degeneracy, and it does so by assumption and not by the data. Third, because the filter keeps the continuous-time trajectories of both drives, the response of a perturbed system relaxing towards its baseline can be described geometrically in the \((x_p, x_s)\) plane (path length, enclosed area, occupied basins); we present these as descriptive summaries of the reconstructed trajectories, not as a fitted potential or an estimate of dissipation. Whether richer dynamics, such as state-dependent noise, time-varying kinetics or coupling between the drives, could be detected from RR intervals alone is an open question that the same identifiability analysis would have to answer first.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
4.7 Limitations
Several limitations delimit the claims. The latent states are model-based reconstructions and are not direct measurements of autonomic neural activity; they have not been compared with microneurographic recordings or tested under pharmacological blockade, and the atropine-informed spectral evidence is external to the present data. Identification remains incomplete even with physiological information. The innovation diagnostics indicated residual serial structure or a departure from the assumed innovation distribution in most recordings (the KS distance was below its critical value in 22% of them), so the reported intervals are conditional on a noise model that holds only approximately. The vagal-like time constant lay inside its 95% prior interval in 19% of recordings, so it should not be read as a strictly vagal time constant: the faster drive may absorb slower fluctuations, such as baroreflex-related oscillations. The recovery times and the time constants of the two drives are shaped by their priors and describe the fitted kinetics; in recordings whose duration is comparable to or shorter than the sympathetic time scale, \(\tau_s\) is likely to be informed mainly by its prior. The hyperparameters are fixed across recordings, the spectral anchor is an approximation, and kinetics and stationary variances are assumed constant within a recording, which may be restrictive during strongly non-stationary exercise. The state intervals are conditional on the MAP parameters, the states are filtered and not smoothed, the optimizer starts from a single point (a local optimum cannot be excluded for an individual recording), and the simulation studies use data generated by the model itself. Finally, the apportioning of a perturbation-induced excursion between the two drives is not determined by the data alone: it depends on the spectral anchor, and in the sensitivity analyses the share of latent variance attributed to the vagal-like process changed by a median absolute 0.10 or more with the vagal floor, the spectral crossover and the \(\tau_p\) prior interval, so statements about the relative contribution of the two drives are conditional on those settings.
The data impose additional limits. Sex and other participant characteristics were not analyzed as covariates. The responses by type of maneuver rest on 20 slow tilts, 20 rapid tilts, 20 stand-ups (at most 2 events of a kind per recording) and are descriptive. The tilt-table dataset comprises a limited number of recordings (10 recordings), each with several tilts that are not independent of one another; events for the recordings without a tilt angle and for the exercise cohort were detected from the same RR series, so timing relative to them is not independent evidence about the states. The Fantasia database includes only group membership as a subject characteristic, and the exercise cohort consists of older adults with a single protocol and no subject-level characteristics or clinical outcomes, so the relevance of the latent trajectories to such outcomes was not evaluated and the behavior of the framework in populations with overt cardiac autonomic pathology remains untested [38,39]. The single-stream formulation does not include respiratory or blood-pressure inputs: respiratory sinus arrhythmia is captured only as an oscillatory component of the vagal state, and baroreflex feedback is implicit [8,40,41], so central autonomic commands cannot be distinguished from peripheral mechanical modulation.

title: SPARK: Physiology-informed inference of latent cardiac autonomic dynamics from RR intervals
text:
4.8 Future directions
The most direct extensions address these limitations. Concurrent respiratory and arterial-pressure signals could be incorporated through explicit coupling terms [42–44], which may reduce reliance on the spectral anchor; validation against microneurography and graded pharmacological blockade [45,46] would test the interpretation of the latent components directly; and hierarchical formulations could learn the hyperparameters across recordings instead of fixing them. Because the continuous-time trajectories are preserved, quantities such as the geometry of the phase-plane path or the behavior of the kinetic parameters near critical slowing down could be explored [47,48], each requiring dedicated validation before a physiological interpretation. Datasets with clinical and functional outcomes and subject covariates would be required to determine whether the latent trajectories carry information that is relevant in those settings.
